1422.title: Looking back: the Tenth Guru's pen
1422.howItsDone: Sikhs who keep the daily prayers read the Tenth Guru's Jaap Sahib and Tav Prasad Swayye in the morning and his Chaupai within the evening Rehras; the Ardas opens with his stanza from Chandi di Var.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Gurus' teachings: Nanak talking with the yogis, the Gurus' different voices, the Ninth Guru's calm. Your line was many voices.

Before sunrise, in a Sikh home, someone is reading quickly. The lines are short, and they land like footsteps: no mark, no sign, no caste, no lineage. That's the Jaap Sahib, from the pen of Guru Gobind Singh. That evening the family stands for the Ardas, and its opening lines are his too. At an amrit ceremony, his words are read over the water as it's stirred. This year gave a whole block to his writings: praise, a life story, a letter of rebuke, a love song. Today, not a shelf of books, but a voice still heard in a Sikh's day.
screen: `BEFORE SUNRISE: SHORT LINES, LIKE FOOTSTEPS.` → `EVENING: THE ARDAS.` → `THE AMRIT.`

segments.voice: Start at dawn. The Sikh code lists the morning prayers: Guru Nanak's Japji, then two from the Tenth Guru, the Jaap Sahib and the Tav Prasad Swayye. A morning moves from the First Guru's voice to the Tenth's, and his part is praise, name after name for the Timeless One, as if no single name were enough. Then evening. The Rehras, the evening prayer in the code, carries his Chaupai. In paraphrase it begins: protect me with Your own hand, and let the wish of my heart be fulfilled. The warrior who wrote it asks to be held. Then the Ardas, the prayer Sikhs say standing together. It opens with the first stanza of his Chandi di Var: first remember Bhagauti, the divine power, then Guru Nanak and the Gurus after him. Bhagauti can be read as God's power, and some readers also hear the sword in that word. Either way, strength and remembrance open the shared prayer together. Then the amrit. The code names five prayers read as the water is stirred with a double-edged khanda, and three are his: Jaap, the swayyas, the Chaupai. Pen and steel, in one bowl. The life story, the rebuke in the Zafarnama, the song from the wilderness are read and sung too, in katha and kirtan. Looking back, his writings aren't only admired from a distance. They're said aloud, morning and night, in prayer, and over the water of the Khalsa.
screen: `DAWN: JAAP AND THE SWAYYAS.` · `EVENING: THE CHAUPAI.` · `THE ARDAS OPENS WITH HIS STANZA.` · `THREE OF FIVE AT THE AMRIT.` · then, large: `PEN AND STEEL, IN ONE BOWL.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening of the Jaap Sahib, in paraphrase: the One who has no mark and no sign, no caste and no lineage. Say it slowly, once, and notice: all the labels people pin on one another, and the line pins none of them on God. If you pray, let the line be your praise; if not, let it rest in the quiet.
Looking back. Today, at the Tenth Guru's pen: his lines open the morning, fill the evening, begin the Ardas and stir the amrit. Today's word.
Your line: pen and sword. A gentle word and a firm one, held in the same hand. Until tomorrow.

1423.title: Looking back: the code
1423.howItsDone: Sikhs look to the Sikh Rehat Maryada for a shared pattern of personal practice, such as the daily prayers, Naam and seva, and of congregational life in the gurdwara, the langar and the amrit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the Tenth Guru's pen: his lines in the morning prayers, the Ardas and the amrit. Your line was pen and sword.

Across a park lawn runs a strip of bare dirt where the grass gave up. Planners call it a desire line. Nobody drew it on a map. Feet made it, one person after another choosing the same way, until the way was visible. A way of life can grow like that. It can also be written down, so the next person doesn't have to guess where the path runs. This year the path walked through one written way, the Sikh Rehat Maryada, a section at a time. Today, a look back at the whole, and why it's fair to call it a way.
screen: `A STRIP OF BARE DIRT ACROSS THE GRASS.` → `FEET MADE THE PATH.` → `A WAY, WRITTEN DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, the code's shape. After it answers who a Sikh is, it sorts Sikh living into two sides: a Sikh's personal life, and the life of the panth, the community together. This year's sections hang on one side or the other. Second, the personal side. In paraphrase, the code names three things: meditating on the Name and the scriptures, living by the Gurus' teaching, and serving others. Not first a journey or a uniform: ordinary things, kept every day. The panth side holds the shared shape: the sangat and the gurdwara, the langar, the amrit and the Khalsa's discipline, and the ways the community settles questions together. Third, why the two sides belong together. The code's daily pattern leans on a passage by Guru Ram Das, met early in that block. In paraphrase: whoever calls themselves a Sikh of the true Guru rises early and remembers the Name, and keeps the Guru's word through the day. Then the passage turns: Nanak asks for the dust of the feet of the Sikh who remembers the Name and helps others remember it too. One person's morning, then the turn toward others. A code makes that pattern specific enough to share, so strangers can walk it side by side. Fourth, nobody walks a whole path at once. The booklet holds a lifetime, but a day is kept one practice at a time: a morning prayer, a covered head, a shared meal, an hour of seva. Step by step, the page becomes a path, worn in by the people who walk it.
screen: `TWO SIDES: PERSONAL AND PANTH.` · `NAME, CONDUCT, SERVICE.` · `GURU RAM DAS: A SIKH'S DAY.` · `ONE PRACTICE AT A TIME.` · then, large: `THE WAY.`

segments.voice: Choose one of the code's three and stay with it: the Name, repeating Waheguru with each breath if you like; the Gurus' teaching, one line of theirs from this year; or service, one person you could serve and the first small step. If your mind wanders, come back to the same one. If you pray, this can be your prayer.
Looking back. Today, at the code: a written way, with a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time. Today's word.
Your line: the way. A written way, kept by walking it. That's today's step, done.

1424.title: Looking back: the streams
1424.hook: many streams and places, one Guru
1424.howItsDone: Sikhs from many streams travel to historic gurdwaras to remember the Gurus' lives, and in gurdwaras near and far the day begins with the Guru Granth Sahib opened and read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the code: a personal side and a panth side, kept one practice at a time. Your line was the way.

If you could stand in one Sikh place for a single hour, which would it be? Nankana Sahib, where tradition places Guru Nanak's birth. Kartarpur, where tradition says he farmed in his last years. Anandpur, where the Khalsa began. Hemkunt, up among snow and a cold lake. Or somewhere much closer: the gurdwara a short drive away, folding tables stacked against the wall for langar. This year walked through those places, and the many streams of Sikh life that gather in them. Today, a look back at both, and at what runs through all of them.
screen: `ONE PLACE, ONE HOUR.` → `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, ANANDPUR, HEMKUNT.` → `OR THE GURDWARA DOWN THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the streams differ, and that's real. The Udasis kept a life of renunciation. The Nirmalas gave themselves to learning. The Nihangs keep their blue and their old ways of speech. The Namdharis wear white. There are Sindhi devotees of Nanak, Sikh families in Assam, communities shaped by craft and trade, and Sikhs in the West who came to the path as adults. Different dress, tunes and emphases, and nobody had to pretend those differences away. Second, places hold memory. A gurdwara often stands where something happened: a birth, a field worked, a stand taken, a death. Sikhs travel to them to remember, and to sit where the Gurus' story touched the ground. Third, the thread. Walk into one of those halls at dawn. Someone lifts the cloths from the Guru Granth Sahib, and the day begins with its word, in the same Gurmukhi letters. The snow differs, the language of the street differs, the food in the langar differs. The book at the center is the one this path has read all year. Fourth, the Granth gives a line for walking between streams. Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger; I have come to get along with everyone. That's a fair way to visit another sangat: not to rank it or correct it, but to sit down, cover your head, and listen. Many streams, many places. And in the gurdwaras this path visited this year, one Guru open at the center.
screen: `THE STREAMS REALLY DIFFER.` · `PLACES HOLD MEMORY.` · `THE SAME GRANTH OPENED AT DAWN.` · `NO ONE A STRANGER.` · then, large: `MANY STREAMS, ONE GURU.`

segments.voice: Bring one place from this year to mind, or a gurdwara near you: the door, shoes off, head covered, hands washed, the Granth under its canopy. Ask what you'd do first, sit for kirtan, bow, or wash plates in the langar, and stay there a while, doing that one thing. If you pray, carry a prayer in with you.
Looking back. Today, at the streams and the places: real differences, real memories, and the same Granth opened at the center. Today's word.
Your line: many streams. Real differences, one Granth at the center, and no one a stranger. Until tomorrow.

1425.title: Looking back: the thought
1425.howItsDone: Sikhs learn the Gurus' thought by hearing and singing the Granth's hymns and through katha, the spoken explanation of a hymn, often returning to lines like the Mool Mantar and the close of the Japji.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at the streams and the places, with the same Granth opened at the center of them. Your line was many streams.

At the end of a long course, a student is handed a blank card and one instruction: in a single sentence, what did you learn? It can be harder than the exam. For a long block this year, the path put four big questions to the Granth. What is God like? Who am I, really? How should I live? What is this world? A few days ago the path ran back through it at speed. Today, slowly: one line for each question, then the blank card comes to you.
screen: `ONE BLANK CARD.` → `FOUR QUESTIONS.` → `ONE LINE FOR EACH.`

segments.voice: God first. In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan holds two things together. In paraphrase: He Himself is beyond all qualities, and He is with qualities too. Beyond every form, and present in every form. The hymns keep both halves, which is why the Granth can call God formless on one page and Beloved, Friend and Husband on the next. Then the self. In the Asa di Var, a salok of Guru Angad names the trouble plainly. In paraphrase: ego is a long, deep illness, and the medicine is found within it too. Haumai, the I that keeps grabbing the center, isn't the whole of a person. The same self that grabs can learn to let go. Then how to live. Elsewhere in the Asa di Var, Guru Nanak puts a whole ethic in one line. In paraphrase: sweetness and humility, Nanak, are the essence of every virtue and every good. Not a long list of rules: two plain qualities, kept in the voice and in the way a person stands among others. And the world. The Japji's final salok says, in paraphrase: air is the Guru, water the father, and the great earth the mother. The world isn't a waiting room. It's family, and it teaches. Four lines, one shape. It all arrives as poetry, much of it sung, and that matters. Sikh thought isn't a form to sign. It's a set of lines to carry, and to keep turning over.
screen: `GOD: BEYOND QUALITIES, AND WITH THEM.` · `SELF: EGO, AND ITS MEDICINE.` · `ETHICS: SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · `WORLD: AIR THE GURU, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · then, large: `LINES TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Suppose a friend asked you tonight, over tea, what the Gurus teach: not what the books say, but what you would say. Let the four lines go by slowly, beyond qualities and with them, ego and its medicine, sweetness and humility, air the Guru and earth the mother, then wait for your own sentence, a few plain words for where you stand today. If nothing comes, that's an answer too; if you pray, bring the question itself into the prayer.
Looking back. Today, at Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world, each held in a line of the Granth. Today's word.
Your line: what I think now. Where you stand today is worth knowing. That's today, done.

1426.title: Year four close
1426.hook: next year: reading the Granth yourself, and living it
1426.howItsDone: Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib in the gurdwara, at home from a gutka of daily prayers or a full copy, and also from printed or digital editions with Gurmukhi and translation side by side.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back at Sikh thought: God, the self, how to live and the world. Your line was what I think now.

A bookmark sits in a book like a small promise: someone was here, and someone is coming back. All year, this path has been reading around a book. Lines quoted from it, hymns sung from it, people bowing before it all over the map. But mostly the book has come in pieces, a line at a time, in paraphrase. Today year four closes. Tomorrow the bookmark moves, and the path puts the Granth itself into your hands.
screen: `A BOOKMARK IS A SMALL PROMISE.` → `A YEAR AROUND ONE BOOK.` → `NEXT, THE BOOK ITSELF.`

segments.voice: First, the year in one breath. It was called the ways of the Guru. It began with the ragas, the musical moods in which the Granth's hymns are arranged. Then Guru Nanak's longer teachings: the dialogue with the yogis, the poem on the alphabet's letters, the song of the months. Then the Gurus who followed him, and the Ninth Guru's calm. Then the Tenth Guru's writings, the Khalsa and the shared code, the living streams of the panth and its places, and last, Sikh thought. Second, what sat at the center of every block. The ragas are the Granth's own order. The Gurus' teachings are its hymns. The code is built around it, the streams bow before it, and even the thought came as its lines. All year, the Granth was the hub, and the path stood a little way off, describing it. Third, what changes. Year five is called the Granth itself, and living it. It starts small: how to read a page, the small signs on the letters, what a hymn's heading tells you, where its center line sits. Then it walks through the Granth in order, from opening pages to closing ones, a reading a day. Not the whole text; a guided walk. Then it turns to living it, through a whole life. Fourth, one picture from near the Granth's close. In the Mundavani, Guru Arjan describes the book as a platter. In paraphrase: on this platter lie three things, truth, contentment and reflection, and the nectar of the Name too. Whoever eats it, whoever savors it, is set free. Next year, the platter is set down in front of you.
screen: `A YEAR CALLED THE WAYS OF THE GURU.` · `THE GRANTH AT THE CENTER OF IT ALL.` · `NEXT: READ A PAGE, THEN WALK IN ORDER.` · `THE MUNDAVANI'S PLATTER.` · then, large: `NEXT, THE GRANTH ITSELF.`

segments.voice: If you have a gutka, a printed copy or a trusted app, open it to the first page and don't try to read yet: just look at the letters, the lines, the space around them. If you don't have one near you, picture where you'll read, at what hour, from what copy. If you pray, ask to come to it ready.
Year four close. The ways of the Guru, gathered up, and a turn toward the book at the center of them all. Today's word.
Your line: next, the granth itself. A bookmark, and a promise to come back. See you in year five.

1427.title: Coming to the Guru
1427.hook: before a call that matters, you sit up. before the Guru's words, hands are washed and heads covered
1427.tomorrow: what's the little book wrapped in cloth on the high shelf?
1427.howItsDone: In a gurdwara, everyone who enters removes their shoes and covers their head before coming before the Guru Granth Sahib; at home, Sikhs commonly wash their hands and cover their heads before reading Gurbani, from a printed book or a screen.

segments.voice: Year four closed on a promise: next, the granth itself. Here it is. And the first question isn't how to read it. It's how to come to it.
screen: `NEXT, THE GRANTH ITSELF.` → `HOW DO YOU COME TO IT?`

segments.voice: Before a video call that matters, people do small things nobody asked for. Close the other tabs. Check their hair. Sit up. Nobody grades it; it's just how a body says, this one counts. In Sikh homes and gurdwaras there's an older version of that. Before the Guru's words are opened, on paper or on a screen, hands get washed and heads get covered. So, one question for the first day of the year: why wash your hands to read?
screen: `CLOSE THE TABS. SIT UP.` → `HANDS WASHED, HEAD COVERED.` → `WHY WASH YOUR HANDS TO READ?`

segments.voice: Start with what Sikhs say the book is. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh, the Tenth Guru, named the Granth as the Guru after him. So in a gurdwara it isn't handled like a book on a shelf. It rests under a canopy, wrapped in cloth, and the people who come in take off their shoes, cover their heads and bow. Everyone covers their head there, visitors of any faith too. At home the same signs travel with the words: clean hands, a covered head. That sounds like manners. Here's where Guru Nanak turns it. In the Japji he says, in paraphrase: when hands and feet and body are dirty, water washes them clean. When the mind is stained, it's washed by love of the Name. The water is real. It's also a pointer. The hands get ready first, and they remind the mind it's next. Something to tell a friend tonight: Muslim neighbors know this question from the inside. Before prayer they make wudu, a washing, and the instruction is in the Qur'an itself, in Pickthall's 1930 English: "When ye rise up for prayer, wash your faces, and your hands up to the elbows." Shared ground: clean hands before the holy, because the body helps the heart arrive. And one honest difference. For Muslims, wudu is part of the prayer's own law, with its steps set in the Qur'an. For Sikhs, the washing and the covered head are a way of honoring the Guru, a book treated as a living presence, and Guru Nanak points past the water to the Name.
screen: `THE GRANTH, HONORED AS THE GURU.` · `WATER FOR HANDS, THE NAME FOR THE MIND.` · `WUDU: WASHING BEFORE PRAYER.` · `SHARED GROUND, HONEST DIFFERENCE.` · then, large: `COME READY.`

segments.voice: If there's a sink close by, wash your hands slowly, the way you would before holding something precious; if not, rub your palms together as if they were wet. Cover your head with whatever is clean and near: a scarf, a cloth, a hood. Then sit with your hands open in your lap, and let each breath out rinse off one thing the day left on you.
Coming to the Guru. Approaching the Granth ready: hands washed, head covered, and a mind on its way. The first word of year five.
Your line: come ready. Clean hands and a covered head, with the mind right behind them. Year five, day one.

screen: `DAY 1427 COUNTS.` → `READING THE GRANTH · 1 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT'S THE LITTLE BOOK WRAPPED IN CLOTH ON THE HIGH SHELF?`

1428.title: The gutka and the steek
1428.hook: the small book wrapped in cloth on a high shelf: a gutka, and its bigger sibling, the steek
1428.tomorrow: what are the tiny marks hanging off every letter?
1428.howItsDone: Sikhs read the daily prayers (Nitnem) from a gutka, kept wrapped in cloth and stored respectfully, and study the Granth's meaning from steeks, printed or online, which set commentary beside the Gurbani.

segments.voice: A week across the edge of a year. Pen and sword. The way. Many streams. What I think now. Next, the granth itself. And yesterday, coming to the Guru: clean hands, a covered head, and the mind right behind. Come ready.
screen: `PEN AND SWORD · THE WAY · MANY STREAMS.` → `WHAT I THINK NOW · NEXT, THE GRANTH.` → `COME READY.`

segments.voice: Every family has one object nobody is allowed to throw out: a recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting, a watch that stopped long ago. In a Sikh home it might be a small book, wrapped in a cloth, kept up high where nothing gets stacked on top of it. Yesterday's question: what is it? It's a gutka. Small enough for a pocket or a purse, it holds the daily prayers in Gurmukhi: the Japji in the morning, the Rehras in the evening, the Sohila at night.
screen: `THE THING NOBODY THROWS OUT.` → `WRAPPED IN CLOTH, KEPT UP HIGH.` → `A GUTKA: THE DAILY PRAYERS.`

segments.voice: A gutka is small, but nothing in it is small talk. Guru Ram Das says it, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and the Guru is the Word, and inside the Word is all the nectar. So yesterday's care doesn't shrink with the book. Clean hands, a covered head, a cloth around it, a place up high. Now its bigger sibling: the steek. A steek sets the Gurbani on the page and adds commentary beside it, line by line: what the old words mean, how one line leads to the next. The Gurbani stays exactly as it is. The commentary is a helper, not a replacement. That's worth knowing about every explanation, including the paraphrases on this path: they walk you toward the words; they aren't the words. On a phone, a Gurbani app does something like both at once: the Gurmukhi above, a meaning underneath. And here's why the two books belong together. The gutka is for saying the same prayers every day, until they live in your mouth. The steek is for understanding, slowly, one line opened up. One keeps you returning. The other keeps you learning.
screen: `THE WORD IS THE GURU.` · `THE SAME CARE, SMALL BOOK OR BIG.` · `STEEK: COMMENTARY BESIDE THE LINES.` · `ONE TO RETURN, ONE TO LEARN.` · then, large: `SMALL BOOK, BIG WORD.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a gutka, a steek online or a Gurbani app, and rest your eyes on a single line without trying to read it fast: the Gurmukhi letters, the meaning beneath, the space between them. If you can't, hold or look at one small thing you keep for what it means, the way that book is kept. Breathe slowly, and let that one line, or that one thing, be all there is to see.
Gutka. A small book of the daily prayers from the Gurbani, kept with the same care as the Granth's words. The second word of the year.
For the road: small book, big word, kept close and kept high. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1428 COUNTS.` → `READING THE GRANTH · 2 OF 20.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT ARE THE TINY MARKS HANGING OFF EVERY LETTER?`
